title: How to Update Old Articles Without Losing Their Value
content:
An old guide still attracts readers, but its menu path no longer exists. Replacing the publication date and adding a new introduction will not help someone who is stuck at step three. The editorial job is to preserve what remains useful, correct what is wrong, and make the changed guidance easy to recognize.

Start with the reader's task. Open the article as if you had never used the product. Follow each instruction against current primary documentation or a controlled environment you are authorized to inspect. Mark each statement as still valid, changed, uncertain, or obsolete. Keep the old URL and a copy of the original draft so the edit can be reviewed and reversed.

Decide whether to revise, consolidate, or retire

A topic may still matter while the article's approach has aged. If the main task and audience remain the same, revise the existing page. If two pages answer the same question, consider combining their strongest material and redirecting the less useful page with care. If the product or feature no longer exists, say so plainly and point readers to a relevant current path when one exists.

Do not keep incorrect instructions visible merely because the page has history. At the same time, avoid deleting context, examples, or caveats that still help the reader. Preserve stable definitions, original diagrams that remain accurate, and links that still support the claim. Recheck external links individually; a live link can lead to content that changed meaning.

Google Search Central's people-first content guidance asks whether a page gives a satisfying answer and warns against changing dates just to appear fresh. Treat that as an editorial quality principle, not a promise of ranking improvement. A substantial revision should be useful to a person who arrives directly, even without search traffic.

Audit claims at the level of the sentence

Extract volatile claims: interface labels, prices, plan limits, software behavior, security instructions, statistics, and policy requirements. Verify each against the current official source and note the checked date privately. If a claim has no reliable source or no longer helps, remove or qualify it. A stale number is often less useful than an explanation of how to find the current number.

Check screenshots and code examples separately from prose. A screenshot can show a retired interface even when the nearby sentence has been updated. A code sample may use an obsolete API, weak default, or package version. Re-run an authorized local example if feasible and label what was actually tested; otherwise say what the documentation supports without claiming execution.

Review accessibility and mobile readability. A new table might convey a comparison clearly on desktop but create overflow on a narrow screen. Give figures meaningful captions and text equivalents. A content update is also a chance to remove decorative complexity that makes the instructions harder to follow.

Make the revision visible and honest

Google's byline-date guidance recommends visible, accurate publication or significant-update dates and says search systems use multiple signals. Use “updated” only when a meaningful revision occurred, with a brief note explaining what changed if that helps readers. A typo correction does not need a dramatic freshness claim.

Keep a short change log for substantial revisions: which steps changed, what source supports the new behavior, whether examples were retested, and whether older advice has been removed. The public note can be brief; the private editorial record should be detailed enough for the next maintainer.

Preserve attribution and permissions. If the old article quoted or adapted another source, review that material before carrying it forward. Prefer original explanations and links to primary documentation rather than copying long passages into the refreshed page.

Hypothetical revision: account export guide

Hypothetical example: An article explains how to export account data. Its first two steps still work, but the export control moved and the article implies that downloading an archive deletes server copies. The editor checks the provider's current export and deletion documentation, updates the navigation steps, and separates “download a copy” from “request deletion.”

They keep the useful section on verifying the archive, replace the obsolete screenshot, and add a note about what was verified from documentation versus what was tested in a controlled account. They retain the page URL because the reader task has not changed. The example is hypothetical; it is not evidence about a particular provider's interface.

Keep the original reader promise in view during editing. If a page promised a five-minute setup and the current process requires administrator approval, revise the promise as well as the steps. An accurate technical section under a misleading title still wastes the reader's time. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the old workflow to follow the revised page and flag where they must guess.

Old-article update checklist

  • Does the opening still match the question a reader brings?
  • Can every numbered step be followed with current controls?
  • Are screenshots, code, links, and caveats still accurate?
  • Are uncertain or untested claims labeled appropriately?
  • Is the update date tied to a substantive change?
  • Have redirects and duplicate pages been considered without breaking useful paths?

After publication, check the page as a reader on a narrow screen and follow its links. Watch for user feedback that points to a missed step. A refreshed article remains a maintained artifact, not a one-time guarantee. Its value comes from a clear answer, transparent limits, and an editor who knows what needs rechecking next.
excerpt: Update an old article by checking every step and volatile claim, preserving accurate context, and recording substantive changes honestly.

seoDescription: Refresh older guides without losing their value: audit steps, verify current primary sources, retain useful examples, and use update dates only for real changes.

sourceNotes.claims: People-first content quality and warning against superficial date changes.
Visible publication and significant update dates and multi-signal byline date guidance.
